title: ACCESS-Style Practice Test — Form A
overview: A full practice test in four parts: Listening, Reading, Writing, and Speaking. Work calmly and do your best. The questions get a little harder as you go.

sections.title: Listening
sections.directions: You will hear short talks and conversations read aloud. Listen carefully. You may hear each one one time. After listening, answer the question that follows. Choose the best answer.

items.title: Classroom Announcement
items.prompt: Where should students go after the announcement?
items.correct: Correct. The speaker says to go to the gym for the assembly.
items.hint: Listen for the place word near the end of the announcement.
items.support: The location usually comes with the word "go to."
items.extension: What time does the assembly start?

teacher.challenge: Ask for both place and time.
teacher.noTech: Read aloud; students point to the answer.
teacher.prompt: How did you know it was the gym?

script: Attention students. In five minutes, we will have a special assembly. When you hear the bell, please leave your classroom and go to the gym. Bring nothing with you.

items.title: Library Rules
items.prompt: What does the librarian ask students NOT to do?
items.correct: Correct. The librarian asks students not to bring food and drinks.
items.hint: Listen for the words "please do not."
items.support: A rule about what not to do often starts with "do not" or "please do not."
items.extension: What are students allowed to do in the library?

teacher.challenge: Ask for both allowed and not allowed actions.
teacher.noTech: Read aloud; thumbs up/down on each option.
teacher.prompt: Why might food be a problem in a library?

script: Welcome to the library. You may read, use the computers, and return your books here. Please do not bring food and drinks into the library, because they can damage the books.

items.title: Science Lab Materials
items.prompt: Which items does the teacher tell students to get for the experiment?
items.correct: Correct. The teacher lists a beaker, safety goggles, and a thermometer.
items.hint: Listen for the list joined with "and." A ruler was not mentioned.
items.support: When a speaker lists items, track each one and listen for "and."
items.extension: Why do you think goggles are on the list?

teacher.challenge: Add a distractor and ask why it does not belong.

script: Before we begin today's experiment, please get the following materials from the cart. You will need a beaker, your safety goggles, and a thermometer to measure the temperature.

items.title: Steps to Solve a Problem
items.prompt: Put the steps in the order the teacher explains for solving a word problem.

items.text: Check that your answer makes sense.

items.correct: Correct. You followed the order: read, find numbers, choose operation, check.
items.hint: Listen for order words: first, next, then, finally.
items.support: Order words signal each step of the process.
items.extension: Why is checking your answer the last step?

teacher.use: Sequencing item using academic math talk.
teacher.prompt: Which step do students most often skip?

script: Here is how we solve a math word problem. First, read the problem carefully. Next, find the numbers you need.

items.title: Comparing Two Temperatures
items.prompt: Complete the summary of the weather report.

segments.text: On Monday the high was 75 degrees, which was
than Tuesday. By Wednesday the temperature was the

items.correct: Correct. Monday was warmer than Tuesday, and Wednesday was the coolest day.
items.hint: Listen for comparison words: warmer, cooler, coolest.
items.support: Comparatives like "warmer" compare two things; superlatives like "coolest" compare three or more.
items.extension: Which day would you choose for a picnic? Why?

teacher.use: Harder item integrating data and comparison.
teacher.lower: Show the three numbers written down.
teacher.challenge: Add a fourth day and ask for the range.
teacher.noTech: Read aloud; students fill a printed summary.
teacher.prompt: How do you know which day was coolest?

script: Here is the weather report for this week. On Monday, the high temperature was seventy-five degrees. On Tuesday, it was seventy degrees, so Monday was warmer than Tuesday. On Wednesday, the high dropped to sixty-two degrees, the coolest of the three days. Now complete the summary.

items.title: A Student Discussion
items.prompt: What do the two students decide to do for their project?
items.correct: Correct. After discussing options, they agree to make a poster about recycling.
items.hint: Listen to the END of the conversation, where they finally agree.
items.support: In a discussion, the decision usually comes after they weigh choices.
items.extension: What reason did they give for their choice?

teacher.use: Hardest listening item, requires inference from dialogue.
teacher.function: Drawing a conclusion from a conversation.
teacher.lower: Read twice and pause at the decision.
teacher.challenge: Ask students to explain the reasoning.
teacher.prompt: Whose argument was more convincing, and why?

script: Listen to two students plan a project. Maria says, "We could build a model volcano or make a poster about recycling." Daniel says, "A volcano is messy. I think recycling is more important for our school." Maria answers, "Good point. Let's make the recycling poster."

sections.title: Reading
sections.directions: Read each passage on your own. Then answer the questions about it. You may look back at the passage as many times as you need. Choose the best answer or click the correct sentence.

items.title: Finding a Detail
items.prompt: Click the sentence that tells how honeybees communicate where food is.
passage: Honeybees live together in large groups called colonies.
When a bee finds flowers full of nectar, it returns to the hive.
There, the bee performs a special movement called the waggle dance to show the others where the food is.
Other bees watch the dance and then fly straight to the flowers.

sentences.text: Honeybees live together in large groups called colonies.
When a bee finds flowers full of nectar, it returns to the hive.
There, the bee performs a special movement called the waggle dance to show the others where the food is.
Other bees watch the dance and then fly straight to the flowers.

items.correct: Correct. The waggle dance is how bees show others where food is.
items.hint: Find the sentence with the word "dance."
items.support: Scan for the key word "communicate" or a movement that shares information.
items.extension: What do the other bees do after they watch the dance?

teacher.challenge: Find detail and the following action.
teacher.prompt: Why is the waggle dance useful for the colony?

items.title: Vocabulary in Context
items.prompt: Complete the summary using the passage.
passage: Honeybees live together in large groups called colonies.
When a bee finds flowers full of nectar, it returns to the hive.
There, the bee performs a special movement called the waggle dance to show the others where the food is.
Other bees watch the dance and then fly straight to the flowers.

segments.text: A bee finds the sweet liquid called
in flowers, then returns to the

items.correct: Correct. The bee finds nectar and returns to the hive.
items.hint: Reread sentence two for the sweet liquid and the place the bee goes.
items.support: Use the words around the blank to choose the term that fits.
items.extension: What is the difference between nectar and honey?

teacher.prompt: How did the passage help you choose nectar?

items.title: Main Idea
items.prompt: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
passage: Deserts are some of the driest places on Earth, yet many living things survive there.
Cactus plants store water in their thick stems to last through long dry spells.
Some desert animals are active only at night, when the air is cooler.
These special features help plants and animals live where water is scarce.

options.text: Living things have special features that help them survive in dry deserts.
Some animals are active at night.
Deserts are found all over the world.

items.correct: Correct. The whole passage is about how living things survive in dry deserts.
items.hint: The main idea covers the WHOLE passage, not just one detail.
items.support: Details are examples; the main idea is the big point they all support.
items.extension: Name one detail that supports the main idea.
readFor: a detail vs the main idea

teacher.challenge: Have students restate the main idea in their words.
teacher.prompt: How are details and main idea different?

items.title: Cause and Effect
items.prompt: Click the sentence that explains WHY some desert animals come out at night.
passage: Deserts can be dangerously hot during the day.
To stay safe, some animals rest in shade or burrows while the sun is high.
Many of these animals come out at night because the air is much cooler then.
At night they can search for food without losing too much water.

sentences.text: Deserts can be dangerously hot during the day.
To stay safe, some animals rest in shade or burrows while the sun is high.
Many of these animals come out at night because the air is much cooler then.
At night they can search for food without losing too much water.

items.correct: Correct. They come out at night because the air is cooler then.
items.hint: Look for the word "because," which signals a reason.
items.extension: What is the effect of coming out at night, according to the text?
readFor: a reason animals are active at night

teacher.challenge: Identify both the cause and its effect.
teacher.prompt: How do cooler nights help desert animals?

items.title: Inference
items.prompt: Which statements can you infer from the passage?
passage: Liam stood at the classroom door, holding his schedule tightly.
He did not know anyone, and the hallways had felt like a maze.
When a girl named Sara waved and pointed to an empty seat beside her, Liam let out a breath and smiled.
By lunchtime, he and Sara were laughing about their confusing first-day adventures.

options.text: Liam felt nervous at the start of the day.
Liam had attended this school for many years.
Sara helped Liam feel more comfortable.
By lunch, Liam felt more relaxed.

items.correct: Correct. The text shows Liam was nervous, that Sara helped, and that he relaxed by lunch.
items.hint: One choice is the opposite of the text. Liam did NOT know anyone, so he was new.
items.support: An inference is supported by clues, even if the text does not say it directly.
items.extension: What clue tells you Liam felt nervous at first?

teacher.use: Inference item with a narrative passage.
teacher.challenge: Cite the exact clue for each answer.
teacher.prompt: How did the author show Liam's feelings without naming them?

items.title: Author's Purpose
items.prompt: Why did the author most likely write this passage?
passage: Liam stood at the classroom door, holding his schedule tightly.
He did not know anyone, and the hallways had felt like a maze.
When a girl named Sara waved and pointed to an empty seat beside her, Liam let out a breath and smiled.
By lunchtime, he and Sara were laughing about their confusing first-day adventures.

options.text: To explain how to read a class schedule
To tell a story about how kindness can ease a hard first day
To give directions to the cafeteria
To list the rules of the school

items.correct: Correct. The passage tells a story that shows how a kind classmate made a hard day easier.
items.hint: Think about the kind of text. Is it a how-to, a list, or a story?
items.support: Author's purpose is often to inform, to persuade, or to entertain with a story.
items.extension: What lesson might a reader take from this story?
readFor: what the author wants you to feel

teacher.function: Analyzing why a text was written.
teacher.lower: Sort choices by text type first.
teacher.challenge: Compare to the desert passage's purpose.
teacher.prompt: How is a story's purpose different from an article's?

sections.title: Writing
sections.directions: Read each task carefully. Plan your ideas, then write a clear response in complete sentences. Use the word bank and sentence frames to help you. Take your time and check your work.

items.title: Explain a Process
items.prompt: Explain how to take care of a class pet or a plant. Write 4-6 sentences using order words.
items.correct: Good work. A strong response uses order words and clear, complete sentences.
items.hint: Use a different order word for each step and explain why each step matters.
items.support: Structure: first, next, then, finally. Begin each sentence with an order word.
items.extension: Add one sentence about what could happen if a step is skipped.

teacher.lower: Provide a frame for each step.
teacher.prompt: Why is order important when you explain a process?

items.title: State and Support an Opinion
items.prompt: Some schools want to add 20 more minutes of reading time each day. Do you agree or disagree? Write a paragraph that states your opinion and gives two reasons.
items.correct: Good work. A strong response states a clear opinion and supports it with reasons and a conclusion.
items.hint: Start with your opinion, give two reasons with examples, and end with a conclusion.
items.support: Structure: claim, reason one, reason two, conclusion. Use transitions to connect ideas.
items.extension: Add a sentence that responds to someone who disagrees.

teacher.function: Writing a claim with supporting reasons.
teacher.prompt: Which reason do you think is strongest?

sections.title: Speaking
sections.directions: You will be given a topic and a short time to plan. Then you will speak your answer aloud in complete sentences. Use the sentence frames to organize your ideas. Speak clearly and stay on the topic.

items.title: Describe and Explain
items.prompt: Describe your favorite place at school and explain why you like it. Speak 4-5 sentences.
items.correct: Good work. A strong answer describes the place and gives clear reasons.
items.hint: Name the place, describe it, and use "because" to explain why you like it.
items.support: Use the frame "My favorite place is ___ because ___."
items.extension: Compare it to a place you like less.
items.adminScript: Think about your favorite place at school. I want you to describe it and explain why you like it. Speak four or five sentences. You have one minute to plan, then you will speak.

teacher.prompt: What made that place your favorite?

items.title: Give an Opinion with Reasons
items.prompt: Should students choose their own seats in class? Give your opinion and support it with two reasons. Speak 5-6 sentences.
items.correct: Good work. A strong answer states an opinion and supports it with two clear reasons.
items.hint: State your opinion, give two reasons with "because," and end with a conclusion.
items.support: Structure: opinion, reason one, reason two, conclusion.
items.extension: Mention a reason someone might disagree, then respond.
items.adminScript: Think about whether students should choose their own seats in class. I want your opinion. Speak five or six sentences. State your opinion and give two reasons using the word because. Finish with a conclusion. You have two minutes to plan, then you will speak.

teacher.use: Final speaking task, opinion with support.
teacher.function: Stating and defending an opinion orally.
teacher.prompt: What reason was most convincing to you?
